narrative:
The model estimates there’s a 75% chance you won’t pass your final year, which is well above the 10% threshold that triggers the requirement for extra help. Because of this high risk, you’re now obliged to take remedial courses to give you the best chance of success.

The single biggest reason the model is concerned is that you’ve said you don’t plan to continue your education after high school. Almost every other student in your school has expressed a desire to go on to university or further training, so this goal stands out as unusual and is strongly linked to a higher risk of failing. The model also noticed that your mother’s formal education ended at primary school, which is much less common among students who pass their final year. This factor slightly increases the predicted risk. On the positive side, you’ve never failed a class before, and that clean record helps lower the risk a little.

To turn things around, the first step is to talk with your teachers or counselor about setting a clear goal for life after high school—whether that’s college, vocational training, or another path. Even if you’re unsure, simply stating an intention to continue your education can make a big difference. You might also benefit from extra study time each week; most students who pass spend at least two to five hours studying outside of class. Finally, ask your family if they can support your learning at home, since family help is something many of your classmates already receive. These changes can help reduce the risk and put you back on track.
